title: Flight of the Gull Bronze Model
author: Etienne-Jules Marey
description: A bronze model made in Italy from Marey's chronophotographic work analyzing the flight of birds.
image copyrights: Image RMN-Grand Palais (musée d'Orsay)(reproduced with permission)

title: Light Sculptures: Matter of Impermanence
author: Dexter Callender III
description: Glass sculptures designed from photographic captures of light patterns moving through architecture during the day, from a selection of buildings in Boston (USA).
image copyrights: Image Dexter Callender III (reproduced with permission)

title: Staring At Empty Space
author: Lea Wurthmann
description: A physical installation that showcases the 352 electromagnetic captures required by NASA to produce the 1995 Deep Space image.
image copyrights: Image Lea Wurthmann (reproduced with permission)

title: Secchi Disk
author: Angelo Secchi
description: An analog device used to measure water's turbidity levels by immersing a disk in lakes, seas and rivers.
image copyrights: Image Public Domain

title: Cyanometer
author: Horace-Bénédict de Saussure
description: An analog color gradient circle designed to document, in a standardized manner, the different colors of the sky.
image copyrights: Image Collection Musée d’histoire des sciences (CC BY-SA 4.0)

title: Korean Rain Gauge Ch'ŭgugi
author: Joseon kingdom's Research Institute of Astronomy Geography Calendar and Weather
description: Known as the 'most ancient rain gauge in the world', the Korean rain gauge system was one of the first state-wide rain measuring system.
image copyrights: Image Courtesy of the National Meteorological Museum of Korea

title: Nilometer
author: Civil engineers of Ancient Egypt
description: A specific type of architecture that was built along the Nile for the Egyptian authorities to monitor the level and turbidity of the river.

title: Mesopotamian Clay Tokens
author: Sumerian agriculturalists
description: Accounting tokens that were used for farming goods exchange and accounting in Mesopotamia. The tokens were used for thousands of years and led to the invention of cuneiform writing.
image copyrights: Image of Clay accounting tokens Susa Uruk period - Louvre Museum Paris © Marie-Lan Nguyen (CC BY 2.5)

title: Bulla (Clay Round Seal)
author: Sumerian agriculturalists
description: Clay envelop in which the accounting tokens were initially placed, then only imprinted on.
image copyrights: Image: Globular envelope with a cluster of accounting tokens. Clay - Uruk period. Louvre Museum - Public Domain

title: Westtown Samplers
author: Westtown School - by Girls in Sewing Class
description: Silk globes made by young girls who attended sewing classes at the Westtown School in Pennsylvania, USA.
image copyrights: "Image: Westtown School

title: Monte Sierpe "Band of Holes"
author: Chincha Kingdom & Inca Empire
description: Exceptional topographical site in Peru containing approximately 5,000 regularly spaced holes in the ground, used for goods exchange and accounting during the Inca Empire.
image copyrights: "Image: Monte Sierpe’s holes. © C. Stanish"

title: Inca-Style Khipu
author: Leland L. Locke's book
description: Inca-style khipus illustrating one of the most important book in the history of khipus deciphering, in which L. Locke determined khipus were numerical devices encoded in base 10. The book was published in 1912.
image copyrights: Image:A Peruvian Knot Record by Leslie Leland Locke 1912 - Public Domain"

title: Mississippi Embroidered Map
author: Anne Lacambre
description: Reproduced from an ancient atlas for the visually impaired, the map is a tactile, white on white embroidered map of the Mississippi river.
image copyrights: Image: Anne Lacambre, Reproduced with permission

title: Inequalities Quipus
author: Ewa Tuteja
description: "The project compares through two inca-style quipus
slug: the well-being of Latin America and Scandinavia. It encodes gendered data from the OECD Better Life Index."
image copyrights: images/inequality.jpg

title: Crochet Topography
author: Noriko Takahama
description: The artist has created a method to retrieve elevation data and transform them into printed pattern, then used to crochet specific topographies.
image copyrights: Images: Noriko Takahama - Reproduced with permission

title: Aster
author: Grégoire Eloy
description: The Aster books show a fraction of the 1 million sattelite pictures taken by scientists for a global study on glaciers into 4,000 printed volumes.
image copyrights: Image: Grégoire Eloy, RVB Books, Reproduced with permission

title: Mattang
author: Marshallese navigators
description: The mattang is an abstract stick chart presentation of how swells refract around an island and meet in a series of nodes. They were used a teaching and mnemonic devices, not for navigation.
image copyrights: Image: from the History of Cartography books, Vol 2, Book 3, p.481, courtesy of the Museum fur Volkerkunde, Berlin.

title: Ammassalik Coastline Sculpture
author: Kunit fra Umivik (Inuit hunter from Greenland)
description: A sculpted guide to a stretch of coast north of Ammassalik, made by a local hunter to explain navigation to the Danish expedition captain Gustav Holm, who later wrote his deep despise for Inuit geographical artefacts.
image copyrights: Image:© Greenland National Museum and Archives

title: Paracas Polychrome Mantle
author: Nazca Culture (central Andes)
description: Ceremonial Paracas mantle encoding territorial, genealogical, and possibly calendrical information.
image copyrights: Image: Brooklyn Museum, John Thomas Underwood Memorial Fund, 38.121

title: A Number Between Zero and One
author: Siah Armajani
description: "A Number Between Zero and One is a conceptual sculpture by Iranian-American artist Siah Armajani
slug: consisting of a stack of paper printouts of an imaginary number—10^-205

title: Jaquard Loom Punched Cards
author: Joseph Marie Jacquard
description: Programmable paper cards linked in sequences to control Jacquard looms, allowing complex textile patterns to be mechanically encoded, stored, and reproduced.
image copyrights: Image: Punched card chains used on Jacquard looms. The photo was taken in 2010 at the abandoned Scranton Lace factory in Scranton, PA, USA. Image courtesy of photographer Christopher Payne.
